implementation_notes: The JDK's own vocabulary is the pattern: the java.util.stream package summary defines a stream pipeline as a source, zero or more intermediate operations (filter, map, flatMap, distinct, sorted) and a terminal operation, states that intermediate operations are always lazy ('executing an intermediate operation such as filter() does not actually perform any filtering'), and adds reduction operations (reduce, collect, sum) plus the reminder that a stream may be operated on only once. That replaces an indexed loop with a result list: collection.stream() plus lambdas or method references for the stages and Collectors for the terminal. Keep the loop where the body mutates shared state, depends on indices, or must be stepped through in a debugger.
code_sketch:
List<String> emails = people.stream()
    .filter(Person::isActive)
    .map(Person::email)
    .distinct()
    .sorted()
    .limit(10)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

int total = orders.stream().mapToInt(Order::amount).sum();  // terminal
pitfalls: A stream can be operated on only once: forking the pipeline or adding a second terminal operation may throw IllegalStateException - keep the source collection, not the stream.
Checked exceptions do not fit the functional interfaces, so a throwing mapper needs a try/catch inside the lambda, an unchecked wrapper, or a different API.
Because the stages are lazy, a chain whose lambdas have side effects does nothing until the terminal operation runs, and any exception surfaces there instead of at the offending stage.

variants.name: Parallel stream pipeline (common ForkJoinPool)
variants.implementation_notes: The same pipeline can be evaluated in parallel by starting from parallelStream() (or calling .parallel()), which runs the stages on the common ForkJoinPool. The package documentation requires associative, stateless, non-interfering functions, notes that processing lazily allows a filter-map-sum chain to be 'fused into a single pass', and warns that stateful intermediate operations such as sorted and distinct may need multiple passes or significant buffering under parallel computation. It replaces the sequential pipeline only for large, independent, CPU-bound work; outside that it is slower and harder to reason about.
pitfalls: Sharing mutable state across parallel stages is a race: accumulate with the collectors or reduce instead of forEach into a shared collection.
Blocking I/O inside a parallel stream occupies common-pool threads and has no backpressure, so it can stall unrelated parallel work.
